source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος· οὐκοῦν ὁ αὐτὸς θεὸς Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ τοῖσδε, δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς· καὶ ὡσπερεὶ τὸ οὐκ ἂν διδόμενον συνάγων τοῦτό φησι· σαφῶς γε τῶν ἀπὸ μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας τοῦτο ὁμολογούντων καὶ τὰ τῆς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις φερομένης κοσμογονίας προσιεμένων ὡς ἀληθῆ περί γε τῶν ἓξ ἡμερῶν καὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης, ἐν ᾗ, ὡς μὲν ἡ γραφὴ λέγει, „κατέπαυσεν“ „ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων ἑαυτοῦ“ ὁ θεὸς ἀναχωρῶν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ περιωπὴν, ὡς δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος μὴ τηρήσας τὰ γεγραμμένα μηδὲ συνιεὶς αὐτά φησιν, ἀναπαυσάμενος, ὅπερ οὐ γέγραπται. περὶ δὲ τῆς κοσμοποιΐας καὶ τοῦ μετ᾿ αὐτὴν ἀπολειπομένου σαββατισμοῦ τῷ λαῷ τοῦ θεοῦ „πολὺς“ ἂν εἴη καὶ μυστικὸς καὶ βαθὺς καὶ „δυσερμήνευτος λόγος.“ εἶτα δοκεῖ μοι τὸ βιβλίον συμπληρῶσαι θέλων καὶ μέγα δοκεῖν εἶναι ποιῶν εἰκῇ προστιθέναι τινὰ, ὁποῖά ἐστι καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸν πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον, ὡς ἄρα λέγομεν τὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι ὡς καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ τὴν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνου διαδοχὴν ὁμοίως αὐτοῖς γενεαλογοῦμεν. ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς ἀλλήλους μὲν ἐπιβουλὴν ἀδελφῶν οὐκ ἴσμεν, τὸν δὲ Κάϊν ἐπιβεβουλευκέναι τῷ Ἄβελ καὶ τὸν Ἠσαῦ τῷ Ἰακώβ· οὐ γὰρ Ἄβελ τῷ Κάϊν ἐπεβούλευσεν οὐδὲ ὁ Ἰακὼβ τῷ Ἠσαῦ· ὅπερ εἰ ἐγεγόνει, ἀκολούθως ἂν εἶπεν ὁ Κέλσος τὰς εἰς ἀλλήλους τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἐπιβουλὰς τὰς αὐτὰς ἡμᾶς Ἰουδαίοις ἱστορεῖν. ἔστω δὲ καὶ τὴν εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἡμᾶς ἀποδημίαν τὴν αὐτὴν λέγειν ἐκείνοις καὶ τὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἐπάνοδον καὶ οὐ φυγὴν, ὡς ὁ Κέλσος νομίζει· τί οὖν ταῦτα συμβάλλεται πρὸς τὴν καθ᾿ ἡμῶν ἢ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων κατηγορίαν; ἔνθα μὲν οὖν ᾤετο χλευάσειν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν Ἑβραίων λόγῳ, φυγὴν ὠνόμαζεν· ὅπου δ᾿ ἦν τὸ πραγματικὸν ἐξετάσαι περὶ τῶν ἀναγεγραμμένων μαστίγων ἐπεληλυθέναι τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, τοῦθ᾿ ἑκὼν ἐσιώπησεν.
thought_title: What we hold in common with the Jews
pass_a_gloss: Then next Celsus says: [Celsus:] therefore (οὐκοῦν) the same God for Jews and for these (τοῖσδε) [Origen:] clearly (δῆλον) meaning the Christians; and as if gathering (συνάγων, inferring) what would not be granted (οὐκ ἂν διδόμενον) he says this: [Celsus:] clearly (σαφῶς γε), those from the great church (μεγάλη ἐκκλησία) confessing (ὁμολογούντων) this and accepting (προσιεμένων) as true (ἀληθῆ) the [things] of the cosmogony (κοσμογονία) current among Jews, at least about the six days and the seventh, [Origen:] in which, as the Scripture says, God 'ceased' (κατέπαυσεν) 'from his works' [Gen 2:2] withdrawing (ἀναχωρῶν) into his own lookout/contemplation (περιωπή), but as Celsus, not having observed (τηρήσας) what is written nor understanding (συνιείς) it, says, having rested (ἀναπαυσάμενος), which is not written. About the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) and the sabbath-rest (σαββατισμός) left remaining (ἀπολειπομένου) after it for the people (λαός) of God [Heb 4:9] there would be 'much' and mystical (μυστικός) and deep (βαθύς) and 'hard-to-interpret (δυσερμήνευτος) word' [Heb 5:11]. Then he seems to me, wishing to fill out (συμπληρῶσαι) the book and making it seem great, to add things at random (εἰκῇ), such as also the [things] concerning the first man (πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος), that we say he is the same as the Jews also, and the succession (διαδοχή) from him we genealogize (γενεαλογοῦμεν) like them. But we do not know a plot (ἐπιβουλή) of brothers against one another (εἰς ἀλλήλους), but Cain to have plotted against Abel [Gen 4:8] and Esau against Jacob [Gen 27:41]; for Abel did not plot against Cain nor Jacob against Esau; which, if it had happened, Celsus would consistently (ἀκολούθως) have said we relate (ἱστορεῖν) the same plots of brothers against one another as the Jews. Let it be that we also tell the same sojourn (ἀποδημία) into Egypt as they and the return (ἐπάνοδος) from there and not flight (φυγή), as Celsus thinks; what then do these contribute (συμβάλλεται) to the accusation (κατηγορία) against us or against Jews? Where then he thought to mock (χλευάσειν) us in the account about the Hebrews, he named [it] flight; but where it was the real matter (τὸ πραγματικόν) to examine about the scourges (μάστιγες) recorded to have come upon Egypt from God [Exod 7-12], this he willingly (ἑκών) kept silent (ἐσιώπησεν).

pass_b_english: Next Celsus says: “So the same God belongs to the Jews and to these people,” plainly meaning the Christians. And as if he were drawing a conclusion that would never be conceded, he says this: “Clearly so, since those of the great church admit this, and accept as true the account of the world’s making that is current among the Jews, at least about the six days and the seventh.” On that seventh day, as Scripture says, God “ceased from his works” (Genesis 2:2), withdrawing into his own exalted contemplation. But according to Celsus, who neither attended to what is written nor understood it, God “rested,” which is not written. About the making of the world, and the Sabbath rest that remains after it for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9), there would be “much to say,” and it would be mystical and deep and “hard to explain” (Hebrews 5:11).

Then, wanting to fill out his book and to make it look large, he seems to me to add certain things at random, such as the matter of the first man: that we say he is the same man the Jews speak of, and that we trace the line of descent from him in the same way they do. But we know of no plotting of brothers against one another. We know that Cain plotted against Abel (Genesis 4:8), and Esau against Jacob (Genesis 27:41); but Abel did not plot against Cain, nor Jacob against Esau. Had that happened, Celsus would have been right to say that we tell the same stories as the Jews about brothers plotting against one another.

Grant too that we speak, as they do, of the same going down into Egypt (Genesis 46:6) and of the return from there (Exodus 12:41), and not of a flight, as Celsus supposes. What, then, do these things contribute to the charge against us or against the Jews? Where he thought he would mock us in the account of the Hebrews, he called it a flight. But where the real business was to examine the scourges which are recorded to have come upon Egypt from God (Exodus 7:14–12:30), that he deliberately passed over in silence.
notes: Attribution: 'οὐκοῦν ὁ αὐτὸς θεὸς Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ τοῖσδε' is Celsus; 'δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς' is Origen's gloss. The words after 'τοῦτό φησι·' ('σαφῶς γε τῶν ἀπὸ μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας... τῆς ἑβδόμης') are taken as Celsus's own, so 'the great church' is Celsus's phrase (contrasted with the sects he lists in 5.61-62); it is possible to read 'σαφῶς γε...' instead as Origen's retort ('though plainly those of the great church admit it'), so the boundary of the quotation is uncertain. Origen contrasts Scripture's κατέπαυσεν ('ceased', Genesis 2:2 LXX 'κατέπαυσεν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ') with Celsus's ἀναπαυσάμενος ('rested'); the English keeps the two verbs distinct. 'περιωπή' (literally a lookout or high vantage point) is used by Origen of God's contemplation; rendered 'exalted contemplation'. Hebrews 4:9 (σαββατισμὸς ἀπολείπεται τῷ λαῷ τοῦ θεοῦ) and Hebrews 5:11 (πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος καὶ δυσερμήνευτος) are woven into Origen's sentence. Celsus evidently claimed Christians share the Jewish stories of brothers plotting against each other; Origen denies that the plots were mutual. The descent into Egypt and the Exodus are narrative references, cited at Genesis 46:6 and Exodus 12:41; the plagues are cited as the whole plague narrative (Exodus 7:14–12:30).

Open doubt (review): 5.59: the end of Celsus's quotation ('σαφῶς γε ... τῆς ἑβδόμης') is kept as Celsus's words, following the raised dot after τοῦτό φησι and the reference in 5.61. It could instead be read as Origen's retort; translator_notes records this.
